summary: This Edmund Optics application note introduces polarization of light and its practical role in optical design. It explains unpolarized, linear, circular and elliptical polarization, p- and s-polarization, and how polarizers and waveplates manipulate polarization. It then surveys applications including glare and hot-spot reduction, contrast and color enhancement, stress evaluation in glass and plastic, chemical identification via stereoisomers, and polarization microscopy.
one_line: Edmund Optics application note introducing light polarization types, polarizer and waveplate manipulation, and imaging, stress-analysis, chemical and microscopy applications.
key_facts: Light is called unpolarized if the direction of its electric field fluctuates randomly in time.
The most common source of polarized light is a laser.
Circular polarization consists of two perpendicular linear components of equal amplitude with a phase difference of π/2.
P-polarized light has an electric field parallel to the plane of incidence, while s-polarized light is perpendicular to this plane.
Brewster's angle is a specific angle of incidence under which only s-polarized light is reflected.
An ideal linear polarizer reduces the initial unpolarized intensity I0 by half, giving I = I0/2.
Malus' law states that transmitted intensity through an ideal polarizer is I = I0 cos²θ, where θ is the angle between the incident linear polarization and the polarization axis.
Ideal waveplates modify existing polarizations without attenuating, deviating, or displacing the beam by retarding one polarization component relative to its orthogonal component.
In Figure 5, a linear polarizer in front of a machine vision camera lens removed glare so an electronic chip could be clearly seen.
Unstressed clear objects between crossed polarizers should yield a completely dark field, while internal material stress rotates polarization and produces transmission variations.
Stereoisomers are molecular compounds with the same type and number of atoms but different molecular arrangements, and they rotate polarized light in different directions.
The stereoisomer limonene is the chemical that gives oranges and lemons their characteristic scents.
In a simple polarization microscope, the analyzer is rotated until its polarization plane is 90° from the polarizer, giving minimum transmission.
A Michel-Levy interference color chart relates the color of a birefringent material to its birefringence and thickness.
